cards.back: Access/accounting, logical access, physical access: who accessed what, and who was physically present.
Device, system, and application events: identifies the component that changed or failed.
Login successes/failures and sensitive actions: proves or rules out a successful brute-force attack.
Flows, sessions, and host activity: which machine contacted which destination.
Data about data: timestamp, sender, recipient, size, hash. Often sufficient to build a timeline.
Vulnerability scans, automated reports, NetFlow/IPFIX, surveillance footage, security tools, dashboards, packet captures.
NetFlow = conversations (who talks to whom); packet capture = exact packet contents.
Memory → connections/processes → caches and unwritten logs → disk → backups and archives.
RAM holds keys, payloads, and fileless processes not found on disk. A reboot erases them.
Copy of RAM at a point in time: encryption keys, injections, established connections, fileless processes.
Sector-by-sector copy of a disk: preserves deleted files, unallocated space, and metadata.
Point-in-time capture of state (VM, storage, configuration): fast, but often less comprehensive than a full image.
Forensic copy of the system allowing offline analysis without altering the original.
Hash, timestamp, source, collector, and log of every transfer: proves evidence was not altered.
Hash verification that files and logs were not tampered with between collection, storage, and presentation.
Employee status, leave, termination, disciplinary context, and support.
Accounting = transactions and fraud evidence; legal = legal basis, notification, and legal hold.
Suspension of destruction even if retention is 30 days: check before any deletion.
Normalize (UTC), filter (host, account, time), correlate (multiple sources), reconstruct the timeline.
Verify NTP, time zone, and clock source before concluding on the order of events.
